newsitem.title: USA: Big Three post quality gains, but Japanese still lead.
newsitem.headline: Big Three post quality gains, but Japanese still lead.

text.p: Despite double-digit initial quality improvements by Detroit's Big Three, Japanese automakers kept a solid grip on their traditional lead in the influential J.D. Power and Associates survey, released Wednesday.

Ford Motor Co. said it had 28 percent fewer defects compared with a year ago, the biggest improvement of all manufacturers in the 1997 model year. Ford's car and light truck products had an average of 81 problems per 100 vehicles vs. 113 problems last year.

The study by the Agoura Hills, Calif.-based research firm measures problems from 89 different areas reported by consumers in the first 90 days of ownership. The 1997 study includes responses from more than 43,000 owners.

The overall industry average for 1997 cars and trucks combined dropped to 86 problems per 100 vehicles from 110 problems a year ago. The 22 percent improvement is the largest since the inception of the study in 1987, and the first time the industry average fell below 100, said J.D. Power.

"I think we're seeing the fruits of the labours of the industry in the early '90s when the industry finally got a grip on improving quality," said Chance Parker, director of product research for J.D. Power.

General Motors Corp. had an average of 97 problems, a reduction of 18 percent from 118 last year. Chrysler Corp., finished the survey with 103 problems, down from 128 a year ago, a decline of 20 percent.
As they have in the past, Japanese automakers dominated the top spots in all categories: parent corporations, vehicle brands and individual nameplates.

Infiniti, Nissan Motor Co. Ltd.'s luxury line, had the best showing of any make, dethroning Toyota Motor Corp.'s Lexus brand. Infiniti owners reported an average of 55 problems, 17 percent fewer than last year. Lexus rose to 57 problems from 54 a year ago.
GM's Saturn was the only domestic brand to make it into the top 10 of vehicles by make. Saturn owners reported an average of 73 defects, 11 percent fewer than last year.
The vehicle line with the worst record was Kia Motors Corp. Ltd. J.D. Power found an average of 275 defects.

On an individual vehicle basis, the Lexus LS400 luxury sedan had the best rating, with 36 problems, 29 percent fewer than last year. Infiniti took the second and third spots with its I30 entry luxury car and its new QX4 compact sport utility.

The Windstar minivan from Ford posted one of the largest quality gains of an individual vehicle. The Windstar had 68 problems -- a 60 percent drop from 1996. Another dramatic improvement was registered by GM's GMC Jimmy, which had 79 problems, down 56 percent.

Bringing up the rear of all individual cars and trucks were two GM minivans. The Oldsmobile Silhouette had the most defects -- an average of 204. That was followed by the Pontiac Trans Sport, which had an average of 197 problems.

Among light truck products, Parker at J.D. Power noted that full-size sport utility vehicles and compact vans are categories with the most defects. However, he said the quality gap between cars and light trucks is narrowing, noting the third-place ranking by Infiniti's QX4.
